lesson.title: The Weak Handshakes Between Molecules
lesson.summary: Intermolecular forces are the attractions that act between separate molecules, and their strength and type depend directly on whether those molecules are polar or nonpolar.
lesson.body:
Once molecules exist as distinct units, the question becomes how they interact with each other, and that is the domain of intermolecular forces. These are the attractive forces that act between neighboring molecules, as opposed to the forces holding atoms together within a single molecule. Intermolecular forces are consistently much weaker than covalent bonds, but they are the reason matter has the physical form it does at a given temperature: they determine whether a substance is a gas, liquid, or solid, and they set its melting point, boiling point, viscosity, and solubility behavior.

The type and strength of intermolecular force present in a substance traces directly back to molecular polarity. Polar molecules, which carry a permanent separation of partial positive and partial negative charge, attract their neighbors through dipole-dipole forces, in which the positive end of one molecule lines up near the negative end of another. Nonpolar molecules have no permanent charge separation to rely on, so at first glance it might seem they should not attract each other at all, yet even nonpolar substances like nitrogen gas or the noble gases can be liquefied at sufficiently low temperature, which shows that some attraction must still exist between them. That attraction is called London dispersion forces, and remarkably it acts to some degree between all molecules, polar and nonpolar alike, arising from temporary, shifting imbalances in electron distribution rather than a fixed dipole.

A useful way to organize these forces is by the strength ranking that will be developed across the rest of this chapter: London dispersion forces are generally the weakest, dipole-dipole forces are stronger, and hydrogen bonding, a particularly strong special case of dipole-dipole attraction, is stronger still. It is important to note immediately, however, that this ranking describes typical relative strength for molecules of comparable size, not an absolute rule; dispersion forces can become the dominant force even in polar molecules once the molecule is large enough, because dispersion forces grow with the number of electrons present. That size dependent exception is explored fully once polarizability is introduced later in the chapter.

Recognizing which intermolecular forces are present in a substance starts with classifying its molecules as polar or nonpolar, exactly as developed in the preceding two sections. A sample made of nonpolar molecules, such as liquid oxygen or liquid methane, experiences only London dispersion forces. A sample made of polar molecules, such as liquid hydrogen chloride, experiences dispersion forces plus dipole-dipole attraction, since dispersion forces are present between essentially all molecules regardless of polarity. This layering, where polar substances get dispersion forces as a baseline plus dipole-dipole forces on top, and potentially hydrogen bonding on top of that, is the framework used throughout the rest of this chapter to predict and explain trends in boiling point across related compounds.
